title: Confusion and very high glucose in an older person — recognising and responding to a time-critical presentation

blocks.text: Confusion and very high glucose in an older person — recognising and responding to a time-critical presentation
AMaC MRCP PACES23 · R5-203 · Station 2, acute consultation · Skills A–G (focus C, E, F, G) · 20 minutes · Prepared 14 October 2026 · Educational simulation; not an official PACES mark scheme.

A 78-year-old living alone is brought in confused after several days of thirst, polyuria and weakness. Point-of-care glucose is very high. Speak to the patient (and accompanying person if applicable), identify immediate risks and explain your management plan. The examiner may provide results on request.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: HOOK — Suspected hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS), potentially with mixed DKA; establish measured or calculated osmolality, ketones and acid–base status.

TRAP — Avoid rapid osmotic shifts that can cause neurological harm. Monitor fluid balance and osmolality and consider VTE prophylaxis, balancing bleeding risk. Escalate impaired consciousness or circulatory compromise.

rows: “I need to check how unwell you are first.”
ABCDE, observations, immediate escalation as needed.
“Your symptoms can signal a serious medical complication.”
History of type 2 diabetes, infection, stroke symptoms, fluid intake and medicines; look for major dehydration and neurological impairment, and check circulation/urine output.
“We will act while tests are underway.”

ABCDE, venous glucose, electrolytes, urea, venous gas, ketones and calculated osmolality; 0.9% sodium chloride replacement and close sodium/osmolality monitoring under JBDS HHS pathway; look for and treat infection or vascular precipitant. Insulin timing depends on ketones and glucose/osmolality response, not a blanket immediate DKA protocol.
“I will tell you what we are monitoring closely.”

blocks.text: Patient is alert enough for brief conversation unless the scenario worsens. Initially anxious; asks “Am I going to be all right?” Share the presenting details when asked. If the candidate dismisses symptoms, express concern that symptoms are worsening. For a deterioration curveball, become confused or collapse; examiner then supplies observations.

“I need to reassess observations and escalate before continuing the routine history.”
“I would treat the suspected emergency while confirmatory testing proceeds.”

“The particular hazard I am watching for is: Avoid rapid osmotic shifts that can cause neurological harm. Monitor fluid balance and osmolality and consider VTE prophylaxis, balancing bleeding risk. Escalate impaired consciousness or circulatory compromise.”

Severe hyperglycaemia with confusion requires emergency assessment for HHS, including serum osmolality and DKA overlap. Replace fluid deficits with monitored 0.9% saline; aim for a gradual osmolality fall, not an abrupt glucose target. Avoid routine immediate high-dose insulin in uncomplicated HHS; JBDS advises insulin once osmolality ceases to fall with fluids unless significant ketonaemia/mixed DKA-HHS is present.

THINK: Confusion and very high glucose in an older person. SAY: take symptoms seriously. DO: ABCDE, tests and timely treatment. NUMBERS: 20-minute simulated consultation. TRAP: Avoid rapid osmotic shifts that can cause neurological harm. Monitor fluid balance and osmolality and consider VTE prophylaxis, balancing bleeding risk. Escalate impaired consciousness or circulatory compromise. FINISH: escalation and monitoring.
